body: The goal: a stranger types one sentence, plays the result from a link, and gets a 20-second clip to share. That is the target, not a result. Today playdough is a contract, four research notes and a landing page.

It is a generator, not an engine. It sits on templates from mise_en_place and a design-brief step that turns a vague idea into a fun core loop before anything is built. A human playtest comes before anything is shared.
So far the useful work is visual: six rendered vignettes testing whether generated art can look deliberate. I learned to settle the look before the pipeline.

body: The target: give it one sentence about any project and it lays out a prep pack on disk, with a chosen template, an asset kit, a context brief and a manifest, before the agent starts. Zero setup steps for the agent is the goal. The tool does not exist yet.
What exists is the intent, a landing page, a manual, and a short list of lessons borrowed from my earlier research repos, including one finding that packing evidence loses more than searching for it.
I learned to write down what a tool is not. It is not an agent harness and not the decision model.

body: A core slice now runs on a working branch: four workers take a round on a small test task, the run is killed with kill -9 mid-round, and it resumes from its event log and still picks a winner, with no finished step re-run. That run used recorded model replies. The target is the same loop (propose, evaluate, critique, verify) on a real task with live models; that demo has not run yet.
The loop itself comes from gauntlet, a small Python harness I built earlier. I am carrying its phases and its resume design as reference, not its code. See other experiments.
I learned that a harness needs durable state first, because model calls fail and long runs get killed.

body: The target is a small model that picks among typed options in an agent pipeline, returns calibrated odds, and beats a big model on speed. It builds on Kev, an open model. A first comparison on 50 held-out prompts: Kev-0.8B on CPU scored 0.88 against 1.0 for Sonnet and ran about 1.3x faster. That sample is too small to call, and the gap is real.
The first experiment has Kev-4B compose shadcn landing pages, then a fine-tune on rubric labels on my shared 3060. It is exploratory and lives on a branch.
My earlier classifiers taught me the most: one scored 44.5% on unseen wording at 97% confidence. Calibration on new phrasing is the real test.

body: The target: an agent and I edit one component on a canvas at once, and the result is a real component file on disk. In the spikes, the two-cursor demo runs; it is not a product and I have not used it for real work.
The spikes are small on purpose and live in separate worktrees. The spec borrows a short list of invariants from my earlier precision-canvas repo and leaves the rest of it behind.
I learned to start from the file format, because files on disk stay the source of truth.

title: other experiments
status_note: Salvage audit, read-only; no old code was moved.
oneliner: Four earlier AI experiments, and what my newer projects kept from them.
role: I audited my own earlier repos for the kitchen: what to carry as a reference excerpt, and what to leave.

hero.alt: Bonfire plate: a flame glyph with callouts

body: I audited my earlier repos before building the kitchen. The default verdict was to leave. Nothing was copied wholesale; only excerpts with a provenance note moved into the new repos' reference docs. Four of them stayed experiments; lmr grew into a project of its own.
gauntlet: a Python harness for propose, evaluate, critique, verify over git worktrees, with resume. Its loop and store design go to bonfire. It was never measured on real model runs.

system-a and system-one-mini: classifier experiments. system-a drifted into labeling a coding agent's next tool. system-one-mini was fast (4.95 ms p50) but scored 44.5% on unseen wording at 97% confidence and its final 86% held only in-domain. I carry those failures into nibble, not the code.
precision-canvas: meant as a component canvas, it became a spec programme with 473 capabilities and no editor. napkin takes a few invariants and checklists.

lmr, an offline QA assistant I first audited here, is now its own project with its own page. It still gave mise_en_place one line, the finding that packing loses evidence rather than retrieval, plus a minimum-difference rule to nibble.
